newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algeria's Ouyahia to stay as prime minister - paper.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's Ouyahia to stay as prime minister - paper.

text.p: Algeria's President Liamine Zeroual is to keep his incumbent Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia in office to bolster government stability after last week's general election, a leading Algerian newspaper said on Monday.
United Nations observers criticised in a statement the conduct of parts of the election in which pro-government parties swept to a majority in the new parliament.

The statement, published by local newspapers on Monday, said some observers had problems moving freely during monitoring the poll, and there were questions over voting by security forces and at mobile polling stations.

El Khabar daily, quoting what it called informed sources, said Ouyahia would hand in his government resignation to Zeroual on Monday shortly after the Constitutional Council endorses Thursday's parliamentary election results.

Zeroual will then reconduct Ouyahia as the head of a new reshuffled government, the paper said, adding that Finance and Oil Ministers Abdelkrim Harchaoui and Ammar Makhloufi are likely to stay in the upcoming reshuffled cabinet.

A senior official told Reuters Zeroual would name a prime minister in the "next hours" but refused to discuss speculation on the new government. He said Zeroual was entitled by the constutition to name a head of government or keep the incumbent one in his job.
The election law asserts that the Council has to confirm or reject the poll results 72 hours after the official announcement of the election results.
The official results, released on Friday, gave the National Democratic Rally (RND), which groups Zeroual's backers, 155 seats in the 380-member National Assembly (lower house).

The Islamist-oriented Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) was placed second with 69 seats. The former ruling National Liberation Front (FLN) ranked third with 64 seats followed by Islamist Nahda Movement with 34 seats.
Secularist Socialist Forces Front (FFS) and Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD) won 19 seats each. Independents and other small political groups shared the remaining seats in the house.
All main political parties complained of electoral irregularities and applied before the Council to look into their documentated complaints.
Party leaders doubt that the Council ruling on some irregularites of the poll raised by opposition will influence the order of the winners in the Assembly.

The U.N. observers statement said: "While observers were able to move without fear or threats, several had difficulties to carry out their work with all the independence and free movement necessary to assess objectively these elections."
The statement said the observers also questioned what happened in the special voting buros, where security forces cast their ballots early.
"The majority of observers who supervised them share the opinion that the process did not provide sufficient guarantees for neutrality and transparency," the statement said.
The U.N. team cancelled a news conference in Algiers on Sunday when they had been due to give their verdict on the election.
Instead, a statement was issued which one of the observers said on Monday was "not about giving a judgment on the fairness of the elections. This is up to the Algerian people".
"It gives facts and observations about the election."

El Khabar said pro-government RND party is most likely to forge alliance with the former sole-ruling FLN party to get a majority in the National Assembly in order to secure stability for the government.
The National Assembly can topple the government if a majority of its members rejects the cabinet programme.
The Assembly will hold a maiden session on June 15 to elect the house speaker, party and official sources said.
Officials said the government would step up reforms, agreed upon with the International Monetary Fund, after the election, including a huge privatsation of state-owned enterprises.
